issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may order a remand only within the circumstances authorized for remand or in an exceptional case where remand is necessary; it should decide the case itself when retrial is unnecessary and the issues can be resolved on the available record.
material_facts: The trial court decided the suit after recording findings on all issues, rather than disposing of it on a preliminary point.
The High Court set aside the decree, framed additional issues, and sent the case back for further trial.
The parties had litigated the readiness-and-willingness issue, and neither party sought to introduce further evidence on the additional issues.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court could decide the issues on the existing material and that no retrial was necessary.
issues.conclusion: The High Court's remand was unsustainable and was set aside; the first appeal and civil revision petition were restored to the High Court for decision.
issues.legal_principle: Order 41 Rules 23 and 23A of the Code of Civil Procedure govern remand after reversal in the specified circumstances; Rule 25 permits a limited reference of an omitted issue or factual question. Inherent power under Section 151 cannot be used to bypass express provisions, except in exceptional cases where remand is necessary ex debito justitiae. An appellate court should avoid an unwarranted remand that unnecessarily prolongs litigation.

rule.if: appeal_from_decree and trial_decided_all_issues and not retrial_required and issues_resolvable_on_existing_record

predicates.appeal_from_decree: An appellate court is considering an appeal from a decree.
predicates.trial_decided_all_issues: The trial court decided the case on its issues rather than disposing of it only on a preliminary point.
predicates.retrial_required: A new trial is necessary to decide the case fairly and satisfactorily.
predicates.issues_resolvable_on_existing_record: The issues can be decided by the appellate court on the material already before it.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a case decided on all issues and no new trial is needed because the appellate court can resolve the issues on the existing record, a remand is unwarranted.

issues.legal_issue: The omission of a specific pleading or framed issue does not require a remand when the parties knowingly litigated the matter, had an opportunity to present evidence, and suffered no prejudice; the first appellate court may decide it on the available record.
material_facts: The trial court did not frame a specific issue on readiness and willingness, but the parties and the trial court addressed whether the statutory requirement had been met.
The parties advanced contentions on that issue, and the trial court adjudicated them.
No party claimed prejudice from the absence of a specific issue or that evidence had been excluded or not allowed.
The High Court had also noted that the defendants had not pleaded the objection concerning compliance with the prescribed forms in their written statement.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could assess the trial court's finding on the available material instead of remanding the case to frame additional issues and conduct a further trial.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16(c) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, concerns pleading and proving readiness and willingness. Under Nagubai Ammal v. B. Shama Rao, the rule against relying on evidence for an unpleaded issue does not apply where the parties went to trial knowing the matter was in issue and had an opportunity to adduce evidence; an omission causing no prejudice may be an irregularity. A first appellate court may decide questions of fact and law arising in the case.

rule.if: first_appeal and formal_pleading_or_issue_omitted and issue_knowingly_contested and evidence_opportunity_provided and not trial_prejudice

predicates.first_appeal: The court is hearing the first appeal in the case.
predicates.formal_pleading_or_issue_omitted: A material matter was not specifically pleaded or was not framed as a separate trial issue.
predicates.issue_knowingly_contested: The parties went to trial knowing that the matter was in dispute and addressed it.
predicates.evidence_opportunity_provided: The parties had an opportunity to present evidence on the matter.
predicates.trial_prejudice: A party was prejudiced at trial by the omission of a pleading or framed issue.

issues.definition: If a first appeal concerns an omitted pleading or issue that the parties knowingly contested with an opportunity to present evidence and without trial prejudice, the appellate court may decide it on the existing record.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may take account of material subsequent events established by admitted or public documentary evidence when reviewing the decision and may mould the relief accordingly.
material_facts: After the trial decree, the competent authority declared that the property was within the applicable land ceiling limits, and the order was later communicated to the vendors.
After the decree, the respondent company was declared sick by the industrial reconstruction body.
The Supreme Court considered both events material, documentary, and almost admitted between the parties.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could receive the relevant documents, take account of the subsequent events when testing the judgment under appeal, and mould the relief as necessary.
issues.legal_principle: A first appellate court may consider material subsequent events supported by relevant documents and may assess the decision in light of those events or mould the relief. Public documents of the kind identified by the Court need not be formally proved.

predicates.first_appeal: The court is hearing the first appeal in the case.
predicates.material_subsequent_event: An event occurred after the decision under appeal and is material to the dispute.
predicates.event_supported_by_admitted_or_public_do: The event is supported by documentary evidence that is admitted or is a public document.

issues.definition: When a material event occurs after the decision under appeal and is supported by admitted or public documentary evidence, the appellate court may consider it and adapt the relief.

issues.legal_issue: A first appellate court deciding whether time was intended to be essential in a contract for the sale of immovable property must apply the presumption against time being essential and assess the parties' intention from the contract and surrounding circumstances.
material_facts: The dispute arose from a contract for the sale of immovable property that made obtaining the required permission by a specified time a condition, with the possibility of mutual extension and a consequence for failure to obtain permission.
The High Court considered earlier authorities but did not consider the Constitution Bench decision in Chand Rani, which the Supreme Court said governed the applicable legal test.
The Supreme Court did not decide whether time was the essence of this particular contract.
issues.conclusion: The High Court ought to have considered the Constitution Bench rule when assessing the contract; the Supreme Court expressed no view on the merits of whether time was essential in this case.
issues.legal_principle: Under Chand Rani v. Kamal Rani, time is not presumed to be of the essence in a contract for the sale of immovable property. An intention to make time essential must be expressed unequivocally; even where time is not essential, performance within a reasonable time may be inferred from the contract's express terms, the nature of the property, and the surrounding circumstances. K.S. Vidyanandam v. Vairavan followed the Constitution Bench rule.

predicates.first_appeal: The court is hearing the first appeal in the case.
predicates.immovable_property_sale_contract: The dispute concerns a contract for the sale of immovable property.
predicates.time_essence_is_disputed: The parties dispute whether the contract made performance by a particular time essential.

issues.definition: For a disputed sale of immovable property in a first appeal, time is essential only if unequivocal intention to that effect is established by considering the contract and the surrounding circumstances.

issues.legal_issue: Setting aside a remand does not deprive the appellate court of power to require additional evidence when the court itself needs it to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause.
material_facts: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's remand and noted that the parties were not seeking to adduce further evidence apart from documents concerning subsequent events.
The Supreme Court clarified that the High Court retained authority to require documents or witnesses if the court itself needed them to decide the appeal satisfactorily.
issues.conclusion: The High Court retained its power to require additional evidence on its own need, notwithstanding that the remand had been set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Order 41 Rule 27(1)(b) of the Code of Civil Procedure permits an appellate court to require additional evidence when it needs that evidence to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause. The power is exercised to meet the court's requirement, not merely a party's request.

predicates.appeal_pending: An appeal remains pending before the appellate court.
predicates.appellate_court_itself_needs_additional_: The appellate court itself considers additional evidence necessary to pronounce judgment or for another substantial cause.

issues.definition: When an appeal is pending and the appellate court itself needs additional evidence to decide it, the court may require that evidence.
